lesson.title: Flipping the Switch: What Depolarization Really Means
lesson.summary: Depolarization is the shift in a neuron's membrane potential from its negative resting state toward a more positive value, and it is the electrical event that can trigger a nerve impulse once it crosses a critical threshold.
lesson.body:
Starting from the resting potential of about negative 70 millivolts, depolarization is simply movement of that voltage toward zero and, potentially, beyond it into positive territory. The name describes exactly what is happening: the membrane's carefully maintained negative polarization is being reduced, or partly undone.

Depolarization happens when channels in the neuron's membrane open and allow positively charged sodium ions, Na+, to flow into the cell. Because Na+ is much more concentrated outside the cell and the inside is negatively charged, Na+ rushes in down both its concentration gradient and its electrical gradient the moment those channels open, the same gradient that the sodium-potassium pump works continuously to maintain. Each Na+ ion that enters adds positive charge to the interior, nudging the membrane potential away from negative 70 millivolts and toward zero. These channels can be ligand-gated, opened directly by a neurotransmitter binding to them at a synapse, or, once a signal is already underway, voltage-gated, opened by the change in voltage itself.

Not all depolarization is the same size or has the same consequence. A small stimulus opens relatively few channels and produces a small, localized depolarization that weakens and fades out within a short distance, much like a ripple dying out on a pond rather than traveling the length of the axon. But if enough depolarizing input arrives together, whether from one strong signal or several smaller ones adding up through the summation process, the membrane potential at the axon hillock can be pushed all the way to threshold, typically around negative 55 millivolts, and that is the point at which a full, self-sustaining action potential is triggered rather than another local ripple.

A concrete example is the excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP, produced when a neurotransmitter such as glutamate binds to a receptor on the receiving neuron and opens Na+ channels there. A single EPSP is usually a small, brief depolarization, nowhere near threshold on its own, but many EPSPs summing together across a busy synapse can accumulate into a depolarization large enough to matter, especially when several arrive close together in time or from several dendrites at once.

Depolarization is the essential first domino in neural signaling. Without a stimulus pushing the membrane potential toward threshold, no action potential fires, and no message moves forward to the next stretch of axon or the next neuron. Something as small as a single ion channel opening for a fraction of a second is, multiplied across billions of neurons, the physical basis of every sensation, movement, and thought a person has, which is why the next step, what actually happens once threshold is reached, deserves its own close look.
